Судя по сказанному во Вступительном рассуждении, не следует ожидать найти в этом Труде Планы и Остатки больших Зданий; мне было бы совершенно невозможно их раздобыть; и я неизбежно впал бы в слишком смелые домыслы, если бы взялся дать им хоть малейшее описание; древние Авторы восхваляли их красоту, но все они хранили молчание о расположении, пропорциях и вообще о каких бы то ни было подробностях.

Памятники, которые мне предстоит описать, неизбежно сводятся к тем, что, не представляя собой больших сооружений, избежали варварства или остались погребёнными под обломками, в оползнях земли и в местах, некогда предназначенных для погребений; оттуда они были случайно извлечены, большею частью для того, чтобы быть перевезёнными в Столицу или в иные места. К такого рода Памятникам относятся Монеты времён Республики; те, что служили денежным обращением при владычестве Королей Франции первой и второй династий и были отчеканены в Марселе; Бронзы, Статуи, Барельефы, орудия Жертвоприношений, Амулеты, Погребальные лампы, Пепельные урны, Надгробные надписи, Гробницы, Слёзницы, Украшения — и вообще всё, что стало мне известно, будь то по моим собственным изысканиям, по сведениям, которые любезно сообщили мне учёные Любители древности, или из чтения их Трудов.

Чтобы вернуть Марселю множество античных предметов и составить из них связный свод, я собрал Рисунки и Гравюры, рассеянные по их Трудам, изображавшие марсельские Памятники; и я без колебаний пользовался познаниями этих Авторов всякий раз, когда их мнение представлялось мне наиболее согласным с истиной.

Переписка, которую я вёл со многими сведущими Любителями, обладающими собраниями древностей, доставила мне возможность вернуть немало вещей, найденных в нашем Отечестве и вывезенных из него для украшения этих Кабинетов; я решался принять их лишь на основании свидетельств наименее сомнительных и наиболее достоверных.

Что же до Памятников, которые прошли перед моими глазами или существуют и поныне, то одни я зарисовал сам, другие поручил зарисовать, предварительно внимательно изучив костюм и все признаки, способные с достоверностью указывать на их марсельское происхождение.

Та лёгкость, с какой Торговля этого Города ежедневно позволяет вывозить Древности из Египта и Леванта, внушила мне справедливую осторожность — дабы не принять за марсельские Памятники, таковыми не являющиеся; и я тщательно отверг множество подобных предметов, которыми владеют некоторые из моих Сограждан. Сколь многим я обязан тем из них, кто соблаговолил содействовать моим изысканиям — советами, сообщением предметов, какими они владели, участием в Гравировании, облегчением доступа в Кабинеты, Библиотеки и некоторые Архивы, — с той приветливостью и редкой дружбой, за которую я обязан гораздо более их любви к Отечеству, нежели моим скромным познаниям. Молчание, налагаемое на меня их скромностью, нисколько не умаляет моей искренней признательности.

Известно, что наука о Древностях почти целиком основана на домыслах и что есть вещи, которые можно объяснить, лишь строя наиболее правдоподобное предположение, если в них не находится решающих признаков или связи с историческими чертами. Есть и такие, что, не давая никакой подобной зацепки, могут быть представлены лишь для удовлетворения взора. Я не счёл нужным исключать последние, хотя их и немало, и лишать их Публики в ожидании, пока кто-нибудь, более удачливый в своих изысканиях, не даст им объяснения; я лишь позаботился сохранить их в этом труде, как в некоем общественном хранилище, способном уберечь их от забвения.

В объяснениях, которые я даю многим из наших памятников, порою осторожно прибегая к собственным догадкам, я вовсе не притязал на то, чтобы избежать критики: и сочту себя обязанным тем, кто станет меня опровергать, если они выскажут суждение, более полезное для открытия истин, касающихся Искусств или Истории нашего Города; именно это было главной целью, какую я имел в виду, издавая это Собрание. «Зачем всё это?» — воскликнут, быть может, те, кого соблазнил эгоизм. Зачем воскрешать столько старых древностей? Какая нам польза знать все эти бесполезные вещи? Довольно знать, кто мы есть, а незнание того, чем были наши Предки, не причинит нам никакого вреда. Цицерон отвечает им за меня: «Nescire quid anteà quàm natus sis acciderit, id est semper esse puerum» — не знать того, что произошло до твоего рождения, значит навсегда остаться ребёнком. (Цицерон, в речи, № 120.)

Примечание. На каждой Гравюре проставлен особый номер, служащий отсылкой к тому же числу, указанному в описании, которое даётся в основном тексте труда. Есть несколько Монет, которые увлечённые Художники, согласившиеся их зарисовать, пожелали изобразить в масштабе, превышающем натуральную величину. В то время я не предполагал, что эти Рисунки, которые я собирал лишь для удовлетворения собственного любопытства, смогут однажды послужить для обнародования, и пренебрёг этой точностью. Трудность же впоследствии вновь раздобыть те самые Монеты, чтобы перерисовать их заново, заставила меня предпочесть гравировать Рисунки такими, какими они у меня имелись; если не считать этого недостатка, они точно воспроизводят предметы, изображённые на Монетах, и я позабочусь оговаривать их действительные размеры, приводя их подробно.
en: There are few Cities that can dispute antiquity with that of Marseille. Still fewer can produce testimonies so authentic to their ancient splendor. Strabo, Pliny, Pomponius Mela, and a number of other Writers of the most distant times, cite the Temples, the public Buildings, and the Monuments of our Homeland, as so many constructions worthy of good taste and knowledge of the Arts, which our illustrious Founders had brought back from Greece. Among these Masterpieces, the Temple of Diana of Ephesus, and that of Apollo of Delphi held one of the foremost ranks; they were situated within the Citadel, according to Strabo. (1) This Author…

as exact in his descriptions as he was a good Geographer, also speaks of the Trophies erected in Marseille. Pausanias, in describing the Temples of Delphi, says that at the entrance of that of Minerva one could see a bronze Statue of this Goddess, which the Marseillais had sent there as an offering; which proves that the Arts were cultivated in Marseille to the point of doing without foreign help to embellish this City. It was from her, according to the testimony of Justin and the illustrious and learned M. de Caylus, that the Gauls received the Arts. Cities in which these arts had less vigor still preserve traces of their past greatness.

Nîmes, Vienne, Arles, Orange, St. Rémy display Amphitheaters, Circuses, Temples, Obelisks and Triumphal Arches. Rome and Athens, those famous Cities, whose upheavals were as great and as numerous as those Marseille may have undergone, still have, in our own day, monuments that escaped the barbarity of their conquerors, to serve as models for our Artists. Marseille, sister of the one and rival of the other, preserves none of these precious marks. The curious Traveler, drawn here by fame, prepares to survey these glorious titles with an eager eye, and finds nothing to satisfy his search. There is not one of these Travelers, however little instructed, who is not tempted to call into doubt the pompous descriptions of the ancients, or to reproach our Fellow-citizens for the dearth of monuments to support them.

What can be the reason for this dearth? or rather, what can have deprived our Homeland of these monuments, once so famous? Why do no traces of them remain? The immoderate zeal of the first Christians seems to me to be the principal cause to which the destruction of the Pagan Buildings must be attributed. Marseille was one of the Cities of the West that first received the Christian Religion into its bosom; it must also have been one of those where the worship of Idols ceased the soonest: although it is probable, from some monuments, that the practice of both Religions subsisted at the same time, Idolatry must soon have yielded to Christianity. A lettered City, containing within it an Academy worthy to rival that of Athens, in which Greek and Roman Youth came to study, receives a new religion. If some of the learned Men distinguished there by the breadth of their learning adopt it, that is enough for its progress to be swifter there than elsewhere; this is what must have happened at Marseille. It was for some time in a state of toleration, and the two religions had free practice, as I shall prove in the body of this work: this is a natural consequence of the knowledge and learning of its ancient Inhabitants. The philosophical spirit acquired through study gives a character of gentleness and amenity, which binds men together, however different in belief. Marseille, however, experienced the horrors of persecution (the great persecutions of the Christians of Marseille were the effect of the fury of the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, around the year 303); imperious rulers made the blood of Christians flow: but as soon as, through its progress, the Christian Religion had become that of the greater number, the worship of Idols could not long subsist, it became the dominant religion.

It is known what zeal animated the first Christians, not only against Idolatry and the Idols, but also against the places intended to pay them homage. Only one of these buildings was preserved in Marseille; it was the Temple of Diana, which served as a Church for a long time, until its excessive age obliged the Marseillais to build, from its debris and on part of the same site, the Church of the Major, (Ecclesia Major), the major, or first Church. The primitive Church at first had only a single assembly of the Faithful in each City; the title of major, or mother, Church was given to it because there was only a single Clergy, and it was from this Body, as from a common mother, that the clergy of the Churches established afterward was drawn. Marseille, for which a single Church sufficed according to these early rites, did not long allow the Temples of Apollo and Minerva to stand, rendered useless by the abolition of their worship, and they were demolished along with everything that had served Paganism, by that ill-conceived zeal which has deprived us of so many other Masterpieces that could have been preserved and put to uses bearing no relation to that which they had served before.

This first period of the establishment of Christianity as the dominant religion in Marseille necessarily had to bring about a revolution in the Arts. The Painters, Sculptors and Engravers, accustomed to earn their living by painting, sculpting, and engraving subjects related to the Pagan Theogony, no longer found employment among the first Christians, who had to regard them as suspect, as people capable of perpetuating through their works what they had an interest in annihilating. These Artists had to leave a place where they were without occupation, to seek employment elsewhere. This scarcity of craftsmen, in the early centuries of the Church, is proven by the poor taste and incorrectness of design that reign in all the works of that time bearing the stamp of Christianity, in which, instead of the rules of art, one sees nothing but the ineptitude of the weakest Pupils. (The Emperor Theodosius having ordered, by Edict, in 389, that all Buildings, Altars, Statues, and everything that had any connection with Paganism be demolished, nothing remained but shapeless debris of all the precious objects of this kind that Marseille contained; thus those we have recovered generally bear, through their mutilation, the evident marks of the zeal our Ancestors put into carrying out this Edict.)
The second cause of the loss of Marseille's ancient Monuments lies in the upheavals this City endured while passing under the rule of various barbarian Peoples, who ravaged it so many times.

The Salyens, Segoregians, Oxybians, and other Gallic tribes had made vain efforts to seize Marseille. It had at times vanquished these peoples with its own arms, at times by combining them with those of its Roman allies, until the unfortunate discord between Caesar and Pompey drew upon it the wrath of the first of these Warriors, who undertook to besiege it. It seems to me pointless to go into the details of this operation; no one is unaware of what gave rise to it, and what its sad consequences were. Caesar, swollen with his successes, stripped the Arsenal; the City's walls were almost entirely ruined by the Besiegers, in the year of the world 4006, 47 years before Jesus Christ.

I even doubt whether they were not set back further, when Crinas the Physician left to the public Treasury a hundred Sesterces to rebuild them; for if the Statue that Councillor de Peiresc had removed in the last century from the Tower of Sauve-terre was that of this Physician, as tradition reported, it was placed there in gratitude for the benefit of the one it represented. The name Turris Salvæ-terræ shows that the ramparts on the land side were not meant to end very far off, since this Tower was intended to keep watch on the land side, as the Tower called Turretta portus did on the sea side. These principles established, the ramparts that passed by the rock or roque des moulins, in whose angle the Tower of the great clock was later built, in 1417, must have joined the Tower of Sauve-terre. The ramparts formerly passed through the ground now occupied by the rue Torte St. Christophle, and the houses north of the Hall of the old Fish-market. They must consequently have ended at the nearest quay; this enclosure can only be later than Caesar's siege: I shall now set out the proofs of this.

The ramparts must previously have lain beyond the rue des Consuls, where, in the last century, the remains of the Temple of Minerva were found. In the earliest centuries of Marseille, King Caraumanus or Caramandus, besieging this City, believed he saw, or pretended to see, Minerva in a dream; on this account he made peace with the Marseillais, and having entered the City, went straight to the Temple of the Goddess, whose Statue he recognized as the very figure he said he had seen in his dream, and presented her with a gold collar. If this Prince entered the City in order to go to the Temple of Minerva, the ramparts must therefore have lain beyond this Temple; so learned a City would not have placed the Temple of Minerva outside its walls. For the reasons set out above, the ramparts built through Crinas's benefaction, being probably the same ones that joined

the Tower of Sauve-terre, the stretches of wall at the roque des moulins, those that passed by the rue Torte, and the Hall of the Fish-market: it would follow from this that they had been set back excessively; and consequently several Monuments and public Buildings that had stood on the abandoned ground were overturned, demolished, or abandoned.

To this first misfortune, Marseille added others like it; the Burgundians, according to some Authors, pillaged and sacked it in 413: I think it pointless to dispute this fact; even supposing it apocryphal, there remain enough sad periods to cite, from which to draw proof of the removal or destruction of Marseillais Monuments. The Visigoths seized this City under their King Euric, in 464, and pillaged and ravaged it. Theodoric, King of the Ostrogoths, took it from these in 508, and did great damage. They in turn handed it over to the Franks. The Lombards pillaged and ravaged it in 576. The Saracens likewise seized it in 923, and as a result of the fury that drove them, joined to zeal for their faith, they sacked and pillaged everything before them; the Churches were treated especially badly, and the Abbey of St. Victor was entirely overthrown. Finally, Alfonso of Aragon was the last to sack Marseille, in 1422; the sack,
says the Historian, lasted three days. A Bull of Martin V, addressed to the Cathedral, states formally that 4000 houses were burned in Marseille on this occasion.

Cassian, Founder of the Abbey of St. Victor, and the Monks of this Monastery, furnish us with the third cause of the loss of Marseillais monuments. If we believe Ruffy, this Abbey was built from the debris of Pagan Buildings; it was ruined several times by barbarian peoples, and rebuilt several times, probably always at the expense of abandoned public Buildings, or their remains, scattered in various parts of the City. The Abbey, as it stands today, bears this out. One sees on every side that it was built and decorated only at the expense of mutilated Pagan Buildings, or their remains gathered with that particular zeal Monasteries show when such objects are left to them.

The Cloister of the Abbey is a Peristyle, entirely formed of columns of different marbles; they do not agree in their proportions; some are even mere fragments of columns. The capitals vary among themselves in form; most represent objects proper to Paganism; some appear to have served to adorn the Temple of some Divinity, or some Building devoted to a use quite opposed to monastic chastity. These capitals are of unequal form and unequal proportions; some are of stone, others of marble: which is proof that they were taken from various Buildings. The same is true of the bases: but what proves even more that these objects were gathered to decorate this place are the modern capitals, which the Workmen building this Edifice made to replace columns for which the original capitals could not be recovered; they are all of a shapeless structure, without taste, arrangement, or design: some are no more than a simple inverted cone, without ornament.

The columns and their capitals that adorn the lower Church are ornaments too fine, too regular, beside the Building itself, for one to doubt that they were not originally made to decorate this place, which is of the coarsest construction; which is certain proof that these precious pieces stood in some other Building, from which they were taken, along with so many other similar objects, whose remains lie scattered in the courtyards and gardens of the Abbey.

If to the degradation of profane Buildings, caused by the eagerness of the Monks of St. Victor to seize their remains to adorn their Monastery, we add that suffered by every place adorned with figures and bas-reliefs, under the Episcopate of Serenus, we shall be less surprised at the loss of Marseillais monuments. This Prelate, whom his virtues otherwise rendered so admirable, to whom sincere repentance, purity of morals, and an exemplary life earned the honors of Christian Apotheosis, moved by a zeal more ardent than enlightened, fell into the errors of the Iconoclasts, and had all the images found in the Churches of Marseille broken. The people, who could only be stirred by the example of an otherwise virtuous Prelate, no doubt went to excess in breaking all the

figures they possessed, or that came before their eyes; which must have struck one of the most disastrous blows against the Arts and their progress, and deprived us of a host of precious objects, which might perhaps today serve as models and as historical evidence.
The lands of which the sea has taken possession reveal to us a fourth cause of the loss of Marseillais monuments.

It is not natural to suppose that our Forefathers would have built a Temple on the very shore of the sea, in such a way that the waves came to beat against its foundations; this would have ruined it in a short time. Yet the Cathedral that replaced the Temple of Diana stands in precisely this situation. Is it not even probable that when it was rebuilt, its foundations were set back, to avoid this inconvenience? There is no doubt on this point, and the remains of the ancient Baptistery, seen scattered in the kitchen gardens of the Provostry house, prove that this Building was abandoned for this reason alone.
According to Strabo, Book 4 of his Geography of Gaul, the Temple of Diana and that of Apollo were situated in the Citadel: In arce est Ephesium, & Apollinis Delphici fanum [so says the translator].

Caesar, in his Commentaries, gives us the situation of this Citadel: Hujus quoque spatii pars ea, quae ad arcem pertinet loci naturâ, & valle altissimâ munitâ, longam & difficilem habet opugnationem (that part of this space which belongs to the citadel is fortified by the nature of the ground and by a very deep valley, and is long and difficult to besiege).

The Temple of Diana and that of Apollo were, according to these authorities, indisputably situated within the Citadel of Marseille, just as the Romans had Temples on the Capitol. Pagan superstition, attaching the fate of the Homeland to the protection of its tutelary divinities, lodged them within the Citadels, so that they might preside over the safety of the Republic from the place where its forces were gathered.

This Citadel stood on very considerable high ground; which could not be said today of the site where the first of these Temples stood, unless we grant that the City once extended further toward the sea, which over time has eaten away a great expanse of land that, sloping down toward the shore, formed that very deep valley cited by Caesar — there being today only a two-toise difference in level between the Cathedral and the sea-shore.

Ruffy, in his history of Marseille, has preserved for us the successive periods at which the ramparts in this part of the City were rebuilt, and each time they were probably set back further. I myself saw, as late as 1747, considerable stretches of wall forming part of the ancient ramparts on the Anse de l'Ourse. They had been abandoned in favor of others built a few toises away: these latter have in turn partly collapsed, from the cemetery of la Charité to the corner of the Carmelite Monastery; and in rebuilding this section, it was necessary to open a gate so that the City's rubble could be dumped there, to protect the ramparts from a further collapse. I shall add to these reflections an authority drawn from the Charters of the Cathedral: it appears from its land-registers that it held feudal rights over the houses of several streets situated beyond the gardens of the Provostry. What has become of these streets and houses? All the Chapter's other feudal rights still exist and are collected; they cannot therefore have been mistaken in error by the former keepers of its Archives. In calm weather one can still make out the remains of Buildings in that space now occupied by the sea below the Provostry, as far as the rock shelf called l'Estel; among other things, the shape of a well, which certainly was not originally built in the sea: it would indeed be absurd to suppose so.

The Port of the Gaulish Gate, or Galle Gate, has not existed for several centuries. It was still in use in 1153 for the inhabitants of the Upper City. Today it is nothing more than a sandy beach, almost entirely exposed to the open sea, owing to the erosion it has caused to the rocks that once supported the ground on the side of the present-day Lazaret; we have seen, and still see today, considerable portions breaking away, despite the dumping of rubble to preserve the road leading to the Lazaret: the same is true of the rocks below the Tower of la Tuerie; continual fissures form there, breaking off considerable masses. This spot had, less than twenty years ago, two basins naturally formed by the sea amid these rocks, where people went to bathe in the heat; they were called the great and the little Cairo. The rocks have since collapsed, and hardly any trace of these basins remains.
From what I have just set out, it follows that the sea, by gradually gaining over time the ground occupied by the City, has consequently deprived us of a great many ancient monuments.

If we add to these considerations those arising from the state of indolence in which Commerce and the Arts lay while Marseille was governed by its own Viscounts, we shall find in this a further cause for the loss of its monuments. Sovereigns concerned only with the smallest interests, who built Monasteries, depleted their inheritances to heap benefactions upon them; some even became Monks of St. Victor themselves. Marseille, often divided among several co-heirs of conflicting interests; the Church, enjoying for a long span of time the right of sovereignty over the Upper City; the continual disputes of this portion with the Lower City; the hatreds and enmities of its inhabitants — all this gives the picture of a complete Anarchy, during which the Arts must necessarily have languished. I seem to see the modern inhabitants of ancient Greece, ceaselessly exposed to the extortions of some new Pasha, no longer cherishing those Arts which their Ancestors carried to such perfection, holding only precarious property, and daily destroying the remains of their former greatness to build their huts with them.

The same must have happened in Marseille. The Château Babon had been given to the Clergy by one of the Viscounts; it was even demolished out of jealousy, because it overlooked the Cathedral. Petty interests of this kind must have arisen at every turn, hastening the total ruin of what remained of Marseille's ancient greatness. These times were followed by others less unhappy, under the rule of the Counts of Provence, and happier still when Marseille and Provence were united to the French Monarchy; but the negligence of its Administrators in preserving the few Monuments that chance brought to light made it easy for the curious to carry them off elsewhere. The Fine Arts did not begin to reappear in Marseille until the Reign of LOUIS THE GREAT, with the establishment of our celebrated Countryman Pierre Puget as Sculptor for the Galleys. This great Artist, a new Prometheus, carried the fire of artistic genius into his Homeland; it was from his workshop that he inspired the Veyriers, the Serres, the Mathiases, the Chastels, and so many others. The Marseillais began to appreciate their works, and to regret the loss of those of their Predecessors from the fine centuries of their Republic.

A few Antiquarians arose in Marseille; but none of them devoted himself particularly to what concerned this City. Various relevant pieces, mixed in their cabinets among a host of antique objects that the ease of Commerce brought them from Egypt and the ports of the Levant, lay as if buried, and were never known to the Public. Foreign Scholars had recovered some of our Inscriptions. Ruffy and Guesnay had done the same; but all of them neglected to form of them a connected series that could present, at a glance, a picture of the manners, customs, dress, and religious worship of the Marseillais: this is what I now propose to accomplish, in answer to the wishes of the Amateurs and good Patriots who urged me to publish researches undertaken since my youth, as a simple pastime, with no thought at first beyond satisfying my own curiosity; but which I am now delighted to devote to my Homeland, preserving for it the memory of its Monuments as they have come to my knowledge, and perpetuating through engraving those that the passage of time degrades more each day.
§PLAN OF THIS WORK.

One should not expect, after the Observations made in the Preliminary Discourse, to find in this Work Plans and Remains of great Buildings; it would have been entirely impossible for me to recover them; and I would infallibly have fallen into conjectures too rash, had I undertaken to give even the slightest description of them; the ancient Authors praised their beauty, but all kept silent as to their layout, their proportions, and generally as to any details whatsoever.

The Monuments I have to describe are necessarily limited to those which, not forming great masses, escaped barbarity, or remained buried under rubble, in landslips, or in places once used for burial; from which they were accidentally brought to light, mostly to be carried off to the Capital or elsewhere. Of this kind of Monument are the Medals of the centuries of the Republic; those that served as Coinage under the rule of the Kings of France of the first and second Dynasties, and that were struck in Marseille; Bronzes, Statues, Bas-reliefs, Instruments of Sacrifice, Amulets, Funerary Lamps, Cinerary Urns, Sepulchral Inscriptions, Tombs, Lachrymatories, Ornaments, and generally everything that has come to my knowledge, whether through my own researches, or through those which learned and curious Scholars have kindly communicated to me, or through reading their Works.

In order to restore to Marseille a host of antique objects, and to succeed in forming a connected series of them, I gathered the Drawings and Engravings scattered through their Works, which depicted Marseillais Monuments; and I did not hesitate to profit from the learning of these Authors whenever their view seemed to me most in keeping with the truth.

A correspondence kept up with several learned Amateurs who possess collections of antiquities has afforded me the advantage of recovering many pieces found in our Homeland and carried away from it to adorn such Cabinets; I decided to adopt them only on the basis of the least suspect and most authentic testimony.

As for the Monuments that have passed before my eyes, or that still exist, I drew some myself and had others drawn, after a careful examination of the costume and of every feature that might bear the certain stamp of belonging to Marseille.

The ease with which Antiquities from Egypt and the Levant can be exported, which this City's commerce affords daily, inspired in me a rightful wariness, so as to avoid adopting as Marseillais Monuments that are not; and I scrupulously rejected a great many objects of this kind owned by various of my Fellow-citizens. How much do I not owe to those among them who deigned to further my researches, by aiding me with their advice, by communicating to me objects they possessed, by contributing to the Engraving, by granting me access to Cabinets, Libraries, and certain Archives, with that affability and uncommon friendship which I owe far more to their love of the Homeland than to my own modest learning. The silence their modesty imposes upon me in no way diminishes my rightful gratitude.

It is known that the science of Antiquities is almost entirely conjectural, and that there are pieces that can be explained only by forming the most plausible hypothesis, when they offer no decisive features or connections with historical facts. There are even some which, offering none of these aids, can be presented only for the satisfaction of the eye. I did not think I should omit these latter, numerous though they are, and deprive the public of them, while awaiting someone more fortunate in his researches who might explain them; I have only taken care to preserve them in this work, as in a public repository that might guard them from oblivion.

In the explanations I give of several of our monuments, sometimes cautiously venturing my own conjectures, I have not claimed to place myself beyond criticism: and I shall consider myself indebted to those who refute me, if they put forward a view that may prove more useful for discovering truths concerning the Arts or the History of our City; this was the principal aim I had in view in publishing this Collection. What is the use of it, those seduced by self-interest may perhaps exclaim? What is the use of reviving so many old Antiquities? What does it matter to us to know all these useless things? It is enough for us to know what we are, and we may, without harm, remain ignorant of what our Forefathers were. Cicero answers them for me: Nescire quid anteà quàm natus sis acciderit, id est semper esse puerum — to be ignorant of what happened before one was born is to remain forever a child. (Cicero, in orat. no. 120.)

Note. A particular number has been placed on each Engraving, to serve as a cross-reference to the same figure marked in the description given in the body of the work. There are a few Medals which the enthusiasm of the Artists who lent themselves to drawing them led them to represent at a scale larger than life. I did not imagine at the time that these Drawings, which I gathered only to satisfy my own curiosity, might one day serve to be given to the Public, and I neglected this exactness. The difficulty I later had in procuring these same Medals again in order to redraw them made me prefer to have the Drawings engraved as I possessed them; this defect aside, they scrupulously preserve the objects represented on the Medals, and I shall take care to forestall any question of scale by giving their dimensions in detail.
